baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Ecological revolutions: tensions between ecology, production and reproduction reshape consciousness of nature, with gender analysed at every level (1987–1990)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Merchant's own statement of the framework, 'The Theoretical Structure of Ecological Revolutions', Environmental Review 11:4 (1987), read in full: 'My thesis is that ecological revolutions are major transformations in human relations with non-human nature. They arise from changes, tensions, and contradictions that develop between a society’s mode of production and its ecology, and between its modes of production and reproduction. Those dynamics in turn support the acceptance of new forms of consciousness, ideas, images, and world views' (pp. 265–266). 'The concepts most useful for this approach to environmental history are ecology, production, reproduction, and consciousness' (p. 267); 'An ecological approach to history asserts the idea of nature as a historical actor' (p. 267); production is twofold, 'reproduction is fourfold, having both biological and social articulations' (p. 270); 'Under capitalist patriarchy, reproduction is subordinate to production' (p. 271). Ecological Revolutions (1989), chapter 1 (reprint, Dolbeare 1996, p. 578): in each revolution 'The relations between men and women through which daily life was maintained and reproduced were radically changed.' In the 1990 JAH round table she writes that Worster's essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and that 'environmental history needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction, which interacts with the other three levels' (p. 1117); shifts of power are 'not only those between indigenous and invading cultures but also those between men and women' (p. 1121). In-period readings: Steinberg (Technology and Culture, 1991, read in full) calls her theorizing, 'especially its integration of gender into the analysis', 'a signal contribution', but adds 'There are painfully few people making history in this book' (p. 399); Cronon (1993) footnotes to Death of Nature and Ecological Revolutions the lesson that one cannot understand how a culture relates to an environment 'without examining the ways it engenders the natural world' (p. 9, n. 18). A contribution, not a founding: she takes Kuhn's and Marx's theories of revolution as 'starting points' and rejects 'the determinism Marx assigns to the economic base' (1987, p. 266), draws reproduction from Meillassoux, Peterson and Bridenthal (pp. 270–271), and adds to Worster's levels rather than replacing them (1990, p. 1117). McNeill (2003, pp. 38–39) is a later reading: the scheme 'has not attracted wide imitation within environmental history'.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: The Death of Nature: the mechanical philosophy's dead, inert nature legitimated manipulation and the domination of nature and women (1980)
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Merchant's own argument, The Death of Nature (1980), read in two author-hosted reprinted excerpts (pages are the reprints'). Introduction (Zimmerman, ed., Environmental Philosophy, 1993): 'The ancient identity of nature as a nurturing mother links women’s history with the history of the environment and ecological change'; we must reexamine 'a world view and a science that, by reconceptualizing reality as a machine rather than a living organism, sanctioned the domination of both nature and women' (p. 269); 'Two new ideas, those of mechanism and of the domination and mastery of nature, became core concepts of the modern world' (p. 270). On Bacon: he 'fashioned a new ethic sanctioning the exploitation of nature', though 'Bacon, of course, was not responsible for subsequent uses of his philosophy'; his courtroom imagery 'treats nature as a female to be tortured through mechanical inventions' (p. 272). Chapter excerpt (Zerzan and Carnes, eds., 1991, from 1980 pp. 192–193, 290–292, 294–295): 'Order and power together constituted control' (p. 36); 'The removal of animistic, organic assumptions about the cosmos constituted the death of nature—the most far-reaching effect of the Scientific Revolution', the mechanical order carrying 'a framework of values based on power, fully compatible with the directions taken by commercial capitalism' (p. 37). In-period reading: Cronon (1993, p. 3): 'Carolyn Merchant joined Worster in bringing an environmentalist perspective to the history of science, but combined it with a more feminist approach to argue in The Death of Nature that western science has harmed nature and women in parallel ways'. Contested: Merchant's 1998 retrospective reports early objections over 'how historical events were related to each other and especially to ideas' and 'the precise relationship between female metaphors that described nature and the social subjection of women' (p. 201). Soble (1995, abstract read) names Merchant among critics who claim 'misogynous sexual metaphors played an important role in the rise of modern science' and 'offers a defense of Bacon'; Pesic (1999, abstract read) holds that 'a close study of his works contradicts' the claim that Bacon advocated torturing nature. Leach and Green (1997, pp. 346, 348) place the book among ecofeminist histories in which 'femininity is linked a priori both “with nature” and “with the past”'; their main target is Shiva. A contribution, not a founding: she credits Hessen, Zilsel, Leiss and Kubrin (1998, pp. 199–200). Merchant's 2006 Isis response is a later reading.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: 'Gender and Environmental History' (1990) called his three levels 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field' but found the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and added 'a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction'

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Histories of the Scientific Revolution and of ideas of nature taken into environmental history
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: History of science supplies environmental history with accounts of how ideas of nature were made and used, here the mechanical philosophy and the domination of nature. The Berkeley retrospective and the reprinted 1980 excerpt document the case mapped; Merchant's own contribution is the separate pair of edges from her person entry (revision 1.131). Pesic’s 1999 abstract supplies a competing reading of Bacon’s metaphor, and Merchant’s 2006 response is a later reading; they document disagreement and do not settle Bacon’s intentions.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Three levels of environmental history (nature, modes of production, ideas), with the capitalist transformation of agriculture as the middle level (1979–1990); and, at the end, the 'Second Earth' of 1500 whose abundance gave 'the false impression that there was no limit' (Shrinking the Earth, 2016, as read by Collomb)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Worster's own statements, in-period first. 'Appendix: Doing Environmental History', The Ends of the Earth (1988), read in an abridged reprint and checked by full-text search of the 1988 edition, whose running heads place the passage between pp. 292 and 294 (Isenberg 2013 cites p. 293): 'There are three levels on which the new history proceeds, three clusters of issues it addresses'; 'The first deals with understanding nature itself, as organized and functioning in past times'; 'The second level in this history brings in the socioeconomic realm as it interacts with the environment. Here we are concerned with tools and work, with the social relations that grow out of that work, with the various modes people have devised of producing goods from natural resources'; the third is 'the purely mental or intellectual, in which perceptions, ethics, laws, myths, and other structures of meaning become part of an individual's or group's dialogue with nature'; together they 'constitute a single dynamic inquiry'. 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990; English text checked in Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature, ch. 4; JAH page as cited by Isenberg): 'most environmental historians seem to have settled philosophically on a position that is at once materialist and idealist', yet the essay turns to 'that middle level, the analysis of modes of production as ecological phenomena' (p. 1091), and proposes that 'the single most important task for scholars in the history of modern agroecology is to trace what Karl Polanyi has called “the great transformation”'. Dust Bowl (1979) had argued: 'Capitalism, it is my contention, has been the decisive factor in this nation's use of nature' (p. 5, as quoted by Cronon 1992, p. 1363; wording confirmed in the 1979 edition). In-period readings: Merchant's 1990 response (read) calls his 'conceptual levels of ecology (natural history), production (technology and its socioeconomic relations), and cognition' 'a significant framework for research and writing in this emerging field', while the essay 'lacks a gender analysis' and environmental history 'needs a fourth analytical level, that of reproduction' (p. 1117). Cronon (1992, read) finds that in Dust Bowl 'the chief agent of the story is not “the pioneers” or “civilization” or “man”; it is capitalism', a plot that 'proclaims an apocalyptic prophecy' (p. 1363). McDean (1986) criticises the generalisation across the Plains (existing source, not re-read). A contribution, not a founding: Worster takes the idea from Aldo Leopold, who 'spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history”' (1988), and McEvoy's ecology, production and cognition triad appeared in the same 1988 volume. Later readings, not evidence for this edge: Isenberg (2013, pp. 88–89) reports White's and Cronon's 1990 objections ('superstructure in the old vulgar Marxist sense'; 'potentially excessive materialism'), whose texts are unread here; McNeill (2003, p. 37) writes of environmental historians' theories that 'The most cogent was probably the one elaborated in slightly different versions by both Donald Worster and Arthur McEvoy', but that such theories 'have sparked no groundswells of enthusiasm'. Period-4 wave 1 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md) (edge_904 revision): Collomb 2017 para. 2 read in full; Shrinking the Earth itself unread; the Origins page (Hall chair from 1989 until retirement) and the AHA award list (2012) read.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Environmental historians cite Leopold's call for 'an ecological interpretation of history' (1949) as a precedent for allying history with ecology, and his essays as a moral and literary voice
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Leopold's text, 'The Land Ethic', A Sand County Almanac (1949), read in two unpaginated transcriptions: 'That man is, in fact, only a member of a biotic team is shown by an ecological interpretation of history. Many historical events, hitherto explained solely in terms of human enterprise, were actually biotic interactions between people and land. The characteristics of the land determined the facts quite as potently as the characteristics of the men who lived on it.' After the Kentucky example: 'Is history taught in this spirit? It will be, once the concept of land as a community really penetrates our intellectual life.' Worster (1990, n. 1) and Wynn (2001, n. 55) cite the history passage at p. 205 of the 1949 edition; a paginated 1949 copy was not seen. In-period readings by historians. (1) Worster, 'Doing Environmental History' (1988), abridged reprint read (Merchant reader, 2012, pp. 2–9; reprint pages): 'Take away plant ecology and environmental history loses its foundation, its coherence, its first step' (p. 5); some scholars speak of 'ecological history' or 'historical ecology', meaning 'to insist on a tighter alliance with the science. Some years back the scientist and conservationist Aldo Leopold projected such an alliance when he spoke of “an ecological interpretation of history.”' (pp. 5–6). He then retells the Kentucky example and quotes Leopold's question about 'the plant succession inherent in this dark and bloody ground' (p. 6). (2) Worster, 'Transformations of the Earth', JAH 76 (1990), read only in Portuguese translation (Ambiente & Sociedade, 2002–03): the essay opens with Leopold, who 'reivindicou uma “interpretação ecológica da História”', and continues 'Levou algum tempo para os historiadores darem atenção ao conselho de Leopold, mas finalmente o campo da história ambiental começou a ganhar forma' (p. 23; gloss: it took historians some time to heed Leopold's advice, but the field of environmental history finally began to take shape). The English wording is unchecked. (3) Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993), read in full: 'Environmental history tries to reconstruct the endless layers of change that we and the earth have traced upon each other. It is the history recorded in Aldo Leopold’s tree rings, the history recorded by the marks of his saw upon the good oak as he cut it down' (p. 19; n. 32, p. 22: 'The echo here is that of Leopold’s “Good Oak,” Sand County Almanac, 6-18'); n. 11 (p. 21): 'At this and several other points in this essay, I trust that readers will hear my echoes of Aldo Leopold's Sand County Almanac'. (4) Cronon's History 901 syllabus (Fall 1994) assigns 'Good Oak' in the session 'Reading the Landscape, Part I' (p. 4) and 'Thinking Like a Mountain' with Part IV, 'The Upshot', beside Nash's Wilderness and the American Mind (p. 6). (5) Nash's Wilderness and the American Mind (1967), checked at contents level only, gives him a chapter, 'Aldo Leopold: Prophet'. Bounded: Worster dates 'the idea of environmental history' to the 1970s and the environmental movement (1988, reprint p. 3), and in 1990 warns that the Kentucky facts need more than 'uma forma simples de determinismo ambiental' (p. 24; gloss: a simple form of environmental determinism). Later reading, not evidence for this edge: Cronon's 2003 afterword (pp. 174–175) recalls 'reading the landscape' workshops 'modeled on a famous course taught by Aldo Leopold as early as the 1930s' and calls the Almanac 'no less a meditation on the history of human interactions with the American land'.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Rural Lower Canada as a feudal, household-centred peasant society, neither routine-bound nor market-rational, into which wage labour in the fur and timber trades was fitted (1981–85); and the rebellion of 1837 as a rural popular movement (1993, known through reviews)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words (Labour/Le Travail 15, 1985, read in full): 'my own view is that agriculture was organized primarily around the satisfaction of family subsistence needs through family production. There were surpluses and a portion of these were sold, but a significant proportion was diverted to priests and seigneurs through feudal exactions' (pp. 18–19); against the commercial reading of Paquet and Wallot, cited in n. 16, 'Feudal peasants or market-conscious farmers? No doubt the debates will continue', while 'none of these social formations were dominated by the capitalist mode of production' (p. 19); 'capitalist enterprise had to adapt itself to the prevailing non-capitalist environment' (p. 20); subdivision of holdings followed 'the introduction of domestic industry or of seasonal waged work in the fur or timber trades' (p. 16). Peasant, Lord, and Merchant (1985) is unread; its publisher describes rural Quebec as 'essentially organized around a feudal society', with 'a pronounced pattern of household self-sufficiency' in three Lower Richelieu parishes (lof_greer_1985). His 1981 Sorel study rejected the 'atavistic mentality' explanation of the rural crisis; that critique of Ouellet is carried by edge_989 and is not repeated here. The Patriots and the People (1993) is unread. Reviewers' words, not his: Dessureault (1998, read for evidence-quebec.md) says it 'brise nettement avec les travaux antérieurs de William H. Parker et de Fernand Ouellet pour qui la paysannerie était essentiellement victime de la crise économique et manipulée par des élites ultranationalistes', finds the struggle fed by 'une forme de républicanisme populaire' (p. 206), places Greer 'dans une perspective marxiste anticolonialiste, héritière de l'œuvre pionnière de Stanley B. Ryerson' (p. 205) and objects that he 'réfute l'existence de clivages socio-économiques à l'intérieur même de la paysannerie' (p. 207); Cardinal (1999) writes that 'à plusieurs reprises, A. Greer s'en prend aux arguments de cet historien' (p. 185). Ouellet's review essay on the book (Histoire sociale / Social History 28, 1995) is unread (browser check), so his reply is not quoted and no fernand_ouellet edge is drawn. Rudin (1995) names Greer among the révisionnistes.

relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (read): Tawney's Agrarian Problem among the works 'On English agrarian change' (p. 42 n. 30); on fines at will as the landlords' lever, 'Tawney, Agrarian Problem, pp. 287–310', pp. 296–300, 307 (p. 62 nn. 76, 78).
